analysis.one_liner: Requires financial counselors serving military members to file annual conflict-of-interest disclosures.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 2024 with 13 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never got a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require financial services counselors who advise service members and their families to submit annual financial disclosures to the Defense Department, so the Department can verify the counselors have no conflict of interest before giving advice. Counselors found to have a conflict would be barred from advising troops until it is resolved, and each military secretary would have to report to Congress annually on how many counselors were screened. The bill never advanced past its referral to the House Armed Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and military families, who often receive financial counseling on or near installations and are frequent targets of high-cost financial products. Verifying that counselors are financially independent of the products they recommend would help ensure the advice they get serves them rather than the seller. Taxpayers also benefit from the annual reports documenting how well the screening works.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every financial services counselor providing counseling on installations to agree to annual financial disclosures, so the Department of Defense can check that the advice given to troops is not steered by the counselor's own financial ties.

Makes conflict-of-interest verification mandatory rather than optional: the Secretary concerned must review each disclosure, and must bar any counselor found to have a conflict from advising service members until it is resolved.

Creates an annual report to Congress on the percentage of counselors screened and found conflict-free, giving lawmakers and the public a way to see whether the protections are actually being enforced.

analysis.who_pays: Financial counselors and the companies that place them on military installations, who would bear the cost of annual disclosures and risk being removed from advising troops if a conflict is found, plus the Defense Department's cost of collecting and reviewing the disclosures and reporting to Congress each year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Financial counselors and firms on base

drawbacks.text: The bill only screens the counselors; it does not itself ban the high-cost loans, insurance, or investment products service members are commonly targeted with, so a clean-disclosure counselor could still recommend a costly product in good faith.

Annual financial disclosures and review would add paperwork for the Defense Department and could discourage otherwise qualified counselors from serving on installations, an honest cost of any screening regime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-aimed oversight bill: annual disclosure and conflict review directly targets the specific problem of counselors whose own finances are tied to the products they recommend to troops. The costs are limited to compliance paperwork and some administrative burden, and the main weakness is scope — it polices the advisor, not the products. The bigger problem is that it never got considered at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Sherrill introduced the bill on April 11, 2024, joined by 13 cosponsors including members of both parties.
That same day it was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial services providers and counselors serving military installations, who keep advising troops without annual conflict-of-interest disclosure or review, and whose conflicts remain unverified.

for.name: Rep. Mikie Sherrill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require annual conflict-of-interest disclosures from financial counselors serving service members.

for.name: 5 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Bacon, Stefanik, Kean, and Molinaro, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it sat from April 2024 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 8 Democrats and 5 Republicans cosponsored — but no votes were ever taken, so no recorded opposition exists to measure the split.

industries.industry: Financial services firms selling products on military installations
industries.note: Banks, insurers, and investment firms that place counselors on or near bases would have to disclose their finances annually, and counselors with conflicts could no longer advise troops. Their interest in keeping undisclosed financial ties runs against the service members relying on impartial advice.

industries.industry: Department of Defense financial counseling programs
industries.note: The Defense Department would gain a mandate and new duties — collecting disclosures, reviewing them for conflicts, barring conflicted counselors, and reporting to Congress annually — along with the administrative cost of doing so.
